segments.body: An engine can achieve an impressive performance figure while suffering damage that requires a major overhaul afterward. The Soviet aircraft examples distinguish a successful high-speed run from a power plant that can repeat it reliably in service. Metallurgy determines whether turbine components tolerate that use and remain reusable. Materials research therefore affects practical aircraft performance as much as the ability to produce a powerful engine in the first place.

evidence.note: High-speed runs followed by engine replacement or overhaul, turbine material limits, and the industrial importance of metallurgical research.

segments.summary: A high-speed run says little about operational usefulness if it consumes the engine's remaining service life.

segments.title: Conscription and the maintenance demands of complex equipment
segments.body: Forces that rely heavily on conscripts have less control over the people entering their ranks and the jobs they receive. That limits how confidently planners can assume that demanding maintenance routines will be followed. Motivation is another consideration when choosing how much engineering complexity a system should impose on its operators. The comparison favors matching equipment requirements to the personnel system that must sustain them.

evidence.note: Personnel selection, assignment, and motivation as constraints on maintaining demanding equipment in a conscript force.

segments.summary: Equipment design has to account for how much control a force has over personnel selection, assignment, and maintenance standards.

segments.title: Why a naval F-22 would require a new airframe
segments.body: A runway arresting hook does not show that an aircraft can withstand repeated carrier landings. Those landings impose impacts that require an airframe designed for the task. An F-22-derived carrier aircraft could share engines and some materials or systems, but saltwater protection would also require hardware changes and corresponding software work. The resulting structure would amount to a new aircraft. The F-35C comparison uses an empty weight roughly 3,000 pounds above the F-35A to illustrate the extra structure involved, including thicker titanium components. One proposed carrier role is a squadron capable of penetrating defenses at the beginning of a conflict.

evidence.note: Runway arresting hooks and the greater structural demands of carrier landings.
F-22 component commonality, saltwater protection, F-35A and F-35C empty weights, and the carrier variant's proposed opening-war role.

segments.summary: The F-22's runway arresting hook does not establish carrier suitability, and common engines or electronics would not avoid a major structural redesign.
segments.question: Could the F-22 be adapted for carrier operations?
segments.answerShort: It would need a substantially different airframe, even if the engines and some systems remained common.

segments.title: Rapid Dragon's airlift opportunity cost
segments.body: The exact combat value of a system untested under wartime pressure remains uncertain. A more immediate constraint is the finite pool of transport aircraft available in a Pacific island campaign. The same aircraft proposed for a Rapid Dragon strike may be urgently needed to resupply dispersed bases and allied positions. Each missile sortie therefore carries an operational opportunity cost even if the launch system itself works as intended.

evidence.note: Scarce transport aircraft assigned to missile strikes are unavailable to resupply Pacific island bases.

segments.summary: In a Pacific island campaign, a transport aircraft assigned to launch palletized missiles is unavailable for the resupply work that keeps dispersed bases operating.

segments.title: A twin-engine F-35 would be a new aircraft
segments.body: Turning the F-35 into a twin-engine aircraft while retaining its capabilities would require extensive engineering changes. A new designation would normally follow because the result would be a different type. A familiar number could nevertheless be retained to make congressional funding easier to obtain. The Super Hornet supplies the comparison: family resemblance and an upgrade label can conceal a substantially new aircraft.

evidence.note: The proposed twin-engine F-35, the scale of redesign, and the Super Hornet comparison about retaining a familiar designation.
The Super Hornet's upgrade label as a means of securing funding for a substantially new aircraft.

segments.summary: Adding a second engine while preserving F-35 capabilities would require extensive redesign; keeping the same name would be a funding choice.
segments.question: Could a larger twin-engine F-35 retain the existing aircraft's capabilities?
segments.answerShort: Doing so would require enough redesign to justify a new aircraft type, even if procurement politics encouraged keeping a familiar designation.

segments.title: Replacing every Essex with a Midway-class carrier
segments.body: Replacing each Essex with a Midway is expected to strengthen American carrier operations late in the war. The assumed improvement includes greater resistance to kamikaze attacks. A Midway facing damage comparable to Franklin's could still be severely damaged, even under the favorable survival prediction.

evidence.note: A hypothetical stronger carrier force, reduced vulnerability to kamikazes, and severe damage still possible in the Franklin comparison.

segments.summary: A fleet of Midway-class carriers would improve late-war American carrier strength and damage resistance, especially against kamikaze attacks.
segments.question: What if every Essex-class carrier were replaced one-for-one by a Midway-class ship?
segments.answerShort: The expected result is a stronger late-war carrier force with greater resistance to kamikaze damage.

segments.title: What an F-15N design study establishes
segments.body: Converting the F-15 for carrier service would require rebuilding its airframe around the loads of deck landings. Even a purpose-built carrier aircraft experiences severe structural wear during those landings. A company can advertise a naval version before completing the engineering needed to make it practical, using the proposal to seek development funding. The criticism of the F-15N proposal concerns how much engineering lay behind the offer: a brochure establishes less than a detailed design study.

evidence.note: Carrier landing loads, the need to redesign the F-15 airframe, and the distinction between preliminary proposals and detailed engineering.

segments.summary: The F-15N example distinguishes a company's offer to study an aircraft from completed engineering for carrier operations.
segments.question: Does the F-15N design study show that a naval F-15 was a practical conversion?
segments.answerShort: A study alone does not establish that; repeated carrier landings would require extensive airframe redesign.

segments.title: The Flight III Burke and the cost of surface-fleet risk aversion
segments.body: The criticism of Flight III is that the Burke hull has reached the limits of its expansion while retaining too much of the earlier internal arrangement. A Burke successor based on a larger Zumwalt-derived hull is proposed as an alternative. Surface-ship procurement is judged more risk averse than aircraft development, partly because recent programs have disappointed. Cutting the Zumwalt order spread development costs over only three ships, worsening the apparent cost of each hull. The objection to reusing its design is political: the program's reputation and the Advanced Gun System controversy make congressional approval difficult even if useful engineering could be retained.

evidence.note: Burke growth limits, a proposed Zumwalt-derived successor, and the political effects of program cuts and Advanced Gun System costs.

segments.summary: The Flight III Burke illustrates how repeatedly extending a successful hull can exhaust margins while failed programs make Congress unwilling to fund a cleaner replacement.

segments.title: If Julius Caesar survives the Ides of March
segments.body: Caesar's dictatorship was already moving the Republic toward de facto imperial rule, so his survival would change the route more than the underlying transition. Caesar would still need senior allies and might form a governing partnership resembling a triumvirate with Mark Antony. Cleopatra's relationship or marriage to Antony becomes a major variable. Octavian, the future Augustus, would also have to decide how to respond to Caesarion, Cleopatra's acknowledged son by Caesar. Those relationships leave ample scope for later succession struggles and civil war, while the timing of a formal transition to empire remains unresolved.

evidence.note: Caesar's de facto imperial direction, a possible Antony partnership, and succession conflicts involving Cleopatra, Octavian, and Caesarion.

segments.summary: Caesar's survival changes the personalities and coalitions around Rome's transition, but not the pressure toward de facto imperial rule and another succession conflict.
segments.question: If Julius Caesar survived the Ides of March, would a later triumvirate and civil war still occur, and when would the Republic become the Empire?
segments.answerShort: Rome was already moving toward de facto empire under Caesar, while Antony, Cleopatra, Octavian, and Caesarion would still create powerful coalition and succession pressures.
